title: Blur a Grayscale Grid
statement:
You get a grayscale image as a grid img of whole numbers from 0 to 255. Produce a blurred copy of the same size.

The new value of a cell is the average of the 3 × 3 block centred on it, using only the cells that exist: a corner averages 4 cells, an edge cell 6, an inner cell 9. Round the average down to a whole number.

Every new value is computed from the original image, not from cells you already blurred.

examples.why: Corner: (9 + 0 + 0 + 0) / 4 = 2.25 → 2. Top edge: 18 / 6 = 3. Centre: 36 / 9 = 4. Dividing every cell by 9 would give 1 at the corners.
One row, so each cell only has left and right neighbors: 15 / 2 → 7, 115 / 3 → 38, 108 / 2 → 54.
Each cell's block covers the whole 2 × 2 image, so every average is 100 / 4.

hints: Write the result into a new grid, so blurred values never feed into later averages.
For each cell, loop over row offsets −1..1 and column offsets −1..1, skip positions outside the grid, and keep both a sum and a count.
Integer division of sum by count rounds down for non-negative values. For a big blur radius, a 2-D prefix sum gives every block sum in O(1).

explain.intuition:
This is a box blur, the same filter behind a CSS blur() preview, only with a 3 × 3 box and flat weights. The only care points are the borders, where fewer than 9 cells exist, and the order of updates.

Count the cells you actually add instead of assuming 9, and write into a separate output grid. If you update in place, the cell to the right would average an already-blurred value and the result drifts.
steps: Create an output grid of the same size.
For every cell, visit the up to 9 positions with row and column offsets in −1..1.
Add the values that are inside the grid and count them.
Store floor(sum / count) in the output and return it.
pitfalls: Dividing by 9 everywhere. Border and corner cells have fewer neighbors.
Blurring in place, so later cells see already-changed values.

solutions.title: Visit the 3 × 3 block of every cell
solutions.idea: Sum the in-bounds neighbors and divide by how many there were.

solutions.title: 2-D prefix sums
solutions.idea: Precompute rectangle sums once; each block sum is four lookups and its size comes from the clamped corners. This scales to any blur radius.

followups: Blur in place with only O(1) extra memory. Values fit in 8 bits; where could you hide the new value?
The blur radius becomes k instead of 1. Which solution still runs in O(rows · cols)?
